desc:
Start with the positive integer n and reduce it to 1 using these operations, each of which may be used any number of times:

  • subtract 1, costing a;
  • divide by 2 (only when the current value is even), costing b;
  • divide by 3 (only when the current value is a multiple of 3), costing c.

Return the minimum total cost. If n is already 1 the answer is 0.

Example: n = 10, a = b = c = 1: 10 → 9 → 3 → 1 costs 3. Greedily dividing whenever possible is not always optimal.
hints: Try small n by hand with a = b = c = 1 and check whether always dividing as soon as you can is best. (It is not: with 10, subtracting first wins.)
Every operation makes the number smaller, so the cheapest cost for a value depends only on the cheapest costs of smaller values.
f(1) = 0 and f(m) = min(f(m-1) + a, f(m/2) + b if m is even, f(m/3) + c if m is a multiple of 3). Fill f from 2 up to n.
editorial: Let f(m) be the cheapest cost to turn m into 1. The first operation applied to m produces m-1, m/2 or m/3 (when legal), and the rest of the route is an optimal route from that value. Hence f(m) = min(f(m-1) + a, f(m/2) + b, f(m/3) + c) with f(1) = 0, where the last two options exist only when the division is exact.

Greedy choices fail because the cheapest first step depends on what is reachable afterwards: for 10 the division by 2 leads to 5, which then needs a subtraction, while the subtraction to 9 unlocks two divisions by 3. Filling the table in increasing order takes O(n) time and O(n) space. The largest possible answer is under 10<sup>8</sup>, so it fits in 32 bits.
